**What I found when I went to edit.** I inspected view-9, view-1, and view-6 against `nose-hump.png`, `side.png`, and `front-quarter.png`, and diagnosed the hump exactly as the escalation predicted: it was a stand-alone `CapsuleGeometry` parked on a plain cylinder, with a sphere nose 2% wider than the tube. That stack carries three artifacts a 747 never has — capsule end-caps, a lobe/tube seam, and the proud equator ring you can literally see as a collar circling the fuselage in view-6. No dimension nudge deletes a cap or a seam.

**But the file changed under me.** My first Edit was rejected: a concurrent writer had rewritten `plane.js` between my Read and my Edit. It already contained an iter-13 computed-mesh rebuild — a lofted `BufferGeometry` whose cross-section is a smooth-max union of the main lobe with an upper lobe whose prominence is a smoothstep in x. That rebuild had never been rendered or judged. **You have two writers racing on this one candidate file** — worth knowing, because the shots I was given (iter-1) are from the *old* capsule build, not from what's on disk now.

Rather than clobber it, I executed it and measured it. Two results:

**The hump is genuinely good.** Measured off the built mesh (not the comments): crown holds 4.55 from x=20 to x=30, then fairs 4.51 → 4.14 → 3.58 → 3.10 → 3.00, fully merged into the crown by x≈11. With the nose tip at x=35, the deck ends 36% aft of the tip — "around one third." Closed body, zero NaN.

**All the glazing was broken.** Every one of the 74 panes, doors, and upper-deck windows sat at a mean **34.2°** tilt (worst 46.8°) off the true skin normal — a sign error in `addSkinPlate`.
